images.filename: Jhum cultivation in Nokrek Biosphere Reserve Meghalaya India Northeast India 2004.jpg
images.caption:
Northeast India is very rich in biodiversity and is a part of mega biodiversity hotspots in the world. However, these vast natural resources including forests are in continuous threat from anthropogenic activities and natural calamities. This picture was taken from Nokrek Biosphere Reserve in Meghalaya (India) during 2004. Traditional slush-and-burn agriculture, locally known as Jhum cultivation, is very common among the tribal forest dwelling population in Northeast India. The reduction in biosphere is sometimes high, as visible in this picture.

Image Credit: Baharul Choudhury, Concordia University

images.caption:
Hoolock gibbons are two primate species of genus Hoolock in the gibbon family, Hylobatidae.
Hoolocks are the second-largest of the gibbons, after the siamang. They reach a size of 60 to 90 cm and weigh 6 to 9 kg. The sexes are about the same size, but they differ considerably in coloration: males are black-colored with remarkable white brows, while females have a grey-brown fur, which is darker at the chest and neck. White rings around their eyes and mouths give their faces a mask-like appearance.

The range of the hoolocks is the most northwestern of all the gibbons, extending from northeast India to Myanmar.

images.caption:
In India, State Highways are marked by Milestone markers at regular intervals along the road. These markers indicate the distance travelled and also the status of the road. The Milestone markers are typically rectangular in shape and are painted in green with white lettering.
The green color represents the State Highway, while the text on it denotes the milestone number. For example, if the milestone marker shows "1" , it indicates that the current location is one mile away from the starting point of that particular State Highway.
It should be noted that the actual design and text used on the milestone markers may vary depending on the state and region. However, the overall purpose of the milestone marker remains the same, which is to provide travelers with information about their current location and distance covered on the State Highway.

images.caption: Behdienkhlam is a festival celebrated primarily by the Pnar people of Meghalaya, India. The festival is celebrated annually in July and is an important dance festival of the Jaintia people. The festival is an invocation to God for wading of evil spirits and diseases and blessing for a good harvest.

images.caption: The Nongkrem dance festival is celebrated during Autumn at Smit, the cultural centre of the Khasi Hills. Ka Pomblang Nongkrem dance, popularly known as Nongkrem dance is a festival in Meghalaya performed to appease the all powerful Goddess Ka Blei Synshar for a rich bumper harvest and prosperity of the people.

images.caption: Nongriat, as we all know, hosts the famous Living-root bridges, one which is the only Double-decker bridge known today. Scores of visitors pour down to this beautiful place for years and yet love to revisit again and again. A fascinating journey which consists of about 6500 steps up and down from Tyrna till Nongriat.
